title: Quantization-Triggered Backdoors in Language Models: Cross-Quantizer Transferability and the Validation--Deployment Gap
content:
Computer Science > Machine Learning
  [Submitted on 27 Aug 2026]
    Title:Quantization-Triggered Backdoors in Language Models: Cross-Quantizer Transferability and the Validation--Deployment Gap
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Post-training quantization is often treated as a semantically neutral optimization for edge deployment of Large Language Models. When a full-precision source checkpoint is evaluated and quantization is applied downstream without equivalent re-evaluation, this workflow creates a structural validation--deployment gap: because quantization is a many-to-one mapping over parameter space, source-precision certification does not guarantee behavioral equivalence in the deployed configuration. We formalize this gap through Quantization Behavioral Equivalence Classes (QBECs) and prove that QBEC membership does not imply behavioral equivalence, providing a theoretical basis for quantization-triggered backdoor attacks. Building on a three-stage adversarial fine-tuning framework, we embed latent malicious payloads into models that satisfy the source-precision checks used in our evaluation, yet activate targeted adversarial behavior upon INT8 or 4-bit compression. We evaluate this threat in two operationally motivated scenarios, tactical machine translation and political content analysis, extending prior work from decoder-only causal LMs to multilingual encoder-decoder sequence-to-sequence models. Results show that backdoored translation models move from zero measured friend--foe corruption at repaired FP16 to up to 85.02% inversion after quantization, and that a paired stance classifier measures an ideological shift of up to $\Delta\mathrm{Bias}=0.33$ upon compression. A cross-quantizer transferability analysis further shows that attack persistence varies across quantization schemes and model architectures, rather than being determined by nominal bit-width alone. These findings demonstrate that source-precision auditing alone does not rule out quantization-triggered behavior and that the final deployed configuration must be included in behavioral certification for trustworthy edge AI.

report.summary: Post-training quantization can trigger hidden backdoors in language models, bypassing full-precision safety checks and demanding deployment-time certification.
report.background: Post-training quantization is widely used to shrink large language models for edge deployment, but it is often treated as a semantically neutral optimization. In standard workflows, a full-precision checkpoint passes safety and behavioral evaluation, and then quantization is applied downstream without equivalent re-evaluation. This creates a validation–deployment gap: because quantization maps many parameter states to a single compressed representation, certification at source precision does not guarantee the same behavior after compression. The authors formalize this gap using Quantization Behavioral Equivalence Classes (QBECs), proving that membership in a QBEC does not ensure behavioral equivalence. They then introduce a three-stage adversarial fine-tuning method that plants latent malicious payloads, which remain invisible under FP16 checks but activate under INT8 or 4-bit compression. Observed effects include translation inversion and ideological shifts in stance classification, demonstrating practical risk in real-world deployment pipelines.
key_points: Quantization creates a validation–deployment gap: models certified at full precision may behave differently after compression. Because quantization is many-to-one, source-precision audits cannot guarantee that the deployed artifact is safe, so a separate evaluation of the final quantized model is necessary.

The paper formalizes Quantization Behavioral Equivalence Classes (QBECs) and proves that QBEC membership does not imply equivalent behavior. This theoretical result establishes a concrete foundation for quantization-triggered backdoors, showing that benign-looking full-precision models can contain latent adversarial behavior.

A three-stage adversarial fine-tuning pipeline embeds malicious payloads that survive FP16 checks but activate under INT8 or 4-bit quantization. The attack works on multilingual encoder-decoder models, not just decoder-only LLMs, extending the threat to translation and classification tasks.

In practical scenarios, the backdoored translation model showed up to 85.02% friend–foe inversion after quantization, while a linked stance classifier shifted ideology by up to ΔBias=0.33. These results demonstrate significant behavioral corruption that would go unnoticed by source-precision evaluation.

Attack persistence varies across quantization schemes and model architectures rather than bit-width alone. This cross-quantizer transferability finding means defenders cannot assume a single quantization format is safe, and certification must include the exact deployed configuration.
report.impact: This research exposes a serious blind spot in AI supply-chain security: models that appear safe during development can become malicious after standard quantization, undermining trust in on-device and edge deployments. For developers, it means evaluation pipelines must shift from source-precision-only auditing to quantized-artifact certification, potentially requiring new benchmarks and threat models. For the AI industry, the result challenges the assumption that quantization is purely an efficiency measure, especially for sensitive applications like military translation or political content analysis. Regular users, who increasingly interact with quantized models on phones and embedded devices, may face hidden behavioral risks that are practically invisible to current safety checks. The findings advocate for broader security evaluation across the entire deployment lifecycle, not just the training and pre-quantization stages.
report.tools: Developers can use Hugging Face Optimum and llama.cpp to reproduce quantization workflows and test post-quantization behavior. For adversarial robustness evaluation, the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox (ART) provides methods for testing model resilience. PyTorch’s built-in quantization APIs and NVIDIA TensorRT are useful for exploring INT8 and 4-bit compression schemes. For broader benchmarking, the LM Evaluation Harness can help compare behavior between full-precision and quantized checkpoints across tasks.
